@graph.headline: C-Game to A-Game: Build Your Signature Trading Framework

acceptedAnswer.text: Your C-game is the bottom of your performance bell curve — the specific mistakes you make when you're stressed, tired, or tilted: abandoning the plan, trading on feeling, re-entering right after exiting, sizing errors (too big from overconfidence, too small from fear). It is not bad luck. It is a pattern with a signature — which is why this article's whole point is writing it down.

mainEntity.name: What is my C-game in trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Check your tell list. The classic signs: making errors you'd never make on a good day ("I know I shouldn't do this"), re-entering a position soon after exiting, size mistakes, losing interest after a big mistake. Then match what you see against your C-game card's five tells. Your early-warning signals are personal, which is exactly why you map them yourself instead of borrowing someone else's list.

mainEntity.name: How do I know when I am playing my C-game?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rarely — and forcing it usually makes things worse. The frustration of a failed "reset" is precisely how C-game becomes revenge trading. The realistic move is C-game → B-game: regain control, stop the bleeding, trade mechanically or walk away. A-game returns when its conditions are rebuilt — rest, calm, a fresh session — not when it is forced.

mainEntity.name: Can I jump straight from C-game back to A-game in one session?

acceptedAnswer.text: Counter-intuitively: don't chase the front — pull the back. The inchworm improves by raising the C-game floor; stretching the A-game without fixing the back end just widens your range and ends in snap-back. Making your worst days slightly less bad, week after week, is what actually advances you.

mainEntity.name: How do I improve my A-game?

acceptedAnswer.text: Never compare your A-game to your C-game — that only produces shame. Compare your current C-game to your C-game 1, 3, 6, and 12 months ago: are your worst days less bad? If yes, you're moving forward. If no, you haven't found what causes your C-game yet, and finding it is the work.

mainEntity.name: How do I measure whether I am getting better?

acceptedAnswer.text: Run the traffic-light state audit — the five checks (sleep, stress (your state about the session ahead), recent P&L feeling, life stress (pressures off the desk), physical state) scored green/yellow/red in under five minutes — then size the day to the light. Full plan on green, reduced size on yellow, no trading on red. That is the whole routine; consistency beats duration.

mainEntity.name: What should my pre-market routine include?

acceptedAnswer.text: Run a readiness audit: sleep quality, stress (your state about the session ahead), your feeling about recent P&L (frustration and euphoria are both warnings), life stress (pressures off the desk), physical state. That is the traffic-light audit from this chapter — five checks, under five minutes: multiple red flags means don't trade; one or two means trade at reduced size. Be honest — your account depends on it.

mainEntity.name: How do I assess my emotional state before trading?

acceptedAnswer.text: On process P&L, not money: followed the plan and lost = a good trade; broke the plan and won = a bad trade. Disciplined execution is what compounds improvement over time, not outcomes on any single day. Grade the execution, ignore the rupees, and the journal line stays honest.
